video_title: Mini Brains, Beating Heart Organoids, and the AI That Predicts Them — Fabian Theis, Helmholtz Munich
gist: Fabian Theis (Helmholtz Munich) argues virtual-cell / perturbation-prediction models are finally taking off because perturbation-space data is exploding (organoids, CRISPR screens, 1,000-drug batteries), but warns that linear baselines still win on simple tasks and that the real commercial moat is proprietary data generation plus lab-in-the-loop experiment steering (his new 'Lab Compass' inverse generative model), not platform models alone. He also outlines why Germany/Europe creates startups at US-like rates but fails at Series A/B scaling.

themes.theme: Virtual cell revival driven by perturbation data

insights.claim: Biohub announced a $1.8 billion collaboration with the DOE, NIH, Meta and Google to collect and open-source multiscale biological data for a new generation of virtual cell models, coupled to the Human Cell Atlas consortium.
insights.speaker: RJ Honicky (host) / Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Big-tech and government money is flowing into cell-level biological data, a counterweight to the molecule-design focus of Anthropic/OpenAI biopharma initiatives.
insights.quote: Biohub just announced a $1.8 billion collaboration with the DOE, NIH, Meta, and Google to collect and open-source multiscale biological data that can be used to develop a new generation of virtual cells.

insights.claim: Theis believes generative and lab-in-the-loop methods that worked at the molecule level are now being exported one level up to the cell level, and that perturbation-prediction 'virtual cell' startups are exploding across the US, Europe and China.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Expect a wave of cell-level AI-bio startups, not just structural/molecule design companies.
insights.quote: I think it's a bit exploding there because I think a lot about US Europe, but also in in the Chinese ecosystem there's a lot of of these these additional efforts now happening.

insights.claim: The genuine demand driver for virtual cell models is that pharma desperately needs cell-type context-specific screens, which it cannot yet do; Theis hopes the boom is not just companies bolting AI onto products.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Commercial pull exists from pharma screening needs, but some of the boom may be AI-washing.
insights.quote: pharma is really desperately uh needing to be cell type context-specific in their screens, which at the moment they can't do yet.

insights.claim: Early perturbation models (Theis lab's scGen, 2019) were near-linear shifts in latent space and only did 'okay' because datasets and questions were simplistic; the perturbation space (control vs disease) was far scarcer than the cell observation space.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: The bottleneck for virtual cells has been perturbation diversity, not cell counts.

insights.claim: Perturbation data is now exploding in scale: single experiments measuring 10 million transcriptomes, ~100 cell lines with full CRISPR Perturb-seq, or batteries of 1,000 drugs, which makes rich perturbation prediction possible.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Data-generation vendors and screening platforms are the enabling layer of the virtual-cell trade.
insights.quote: Now you sort of have, I don't know, 100 different cell lines where you do sort of full perturbsic like full CRISPR, or you have like batteries of 1,000 drugs or so added, and suddenly this space gets really rich

insights.claim: Theis defines a perturbation broadly as any input to a cell (cell-cell signaling, hormones, media conditions, gene knockouts, human genetic variation, disease, time and their combinations), and argues a true virtual cell must take all of it, so equating virtual cell with CRISPR perturbation prediction is too simplistic.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Current perturbation-prediction products cover only a narrow slice of the eventual virtual-cell problem.
insights.quote: So, for me a perturbation space in fact is just an input space to stuff that happens to a cell

insights.claim: Theis expects perturbation scaling to eventually extend to using human genetics itself as the perturbation.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Population genetics cohorts could become training data for virtual cell models.
insights.quote: at some point, you know, we're going to go maybe even to human genetics as a perturbation.

insights.claim: Theis is convinced that virtual cell work must move from single cell lines to multicellular systems such as organoids to get really interesting readouts, and his group is running organoid perturbation experiments.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Organoid perturbation platforms are a likely next data frontier beyond cell-line screens.
insights.quote: I'm quite convinced that we need to go to multi-cellular systems to have actually really interesting readouts

insights.claim: Organoids now include mini brains whose neurons connect and can be made to compute, beating heart organoids, colon and cancer organoids, and skin-cell-derived brain organoids for studying neurodegenerative disease where tissue is hard to get; limitations include a missing immune system and no vascular feeding.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Organoids unlock disease models for hard-to-access tissues but are still incomplete biological proxies.
insights.quote: Like you have beating little heart cell clumps in a dish, right?

insights.claim: How to model spatially connected and organoid data is an unsolved research frontier: there is no agreed representation or 'cell type'-like categorization for local cell niches, and current practice treats them as distributions of cells, with graphs a possible improvement.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Spatial/organoid modeling remains open terrain for new methods and companies.
insights.quote: I don't think we have a similar metaphor for local niches of cells.

themes.theme: Bitter lesson vs inductive bias and scaling

insights.claim: Theis says literature has shown over decades that building strong a priori inductive biases into models costs predictive power, but because perturbation-space data is still not in a super data-rich regime, hybrid models remain the right choice in biology for now.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Near-term winners in bio-AI may combine priors with data; pure scale plays need more perturbation data first.
insights.quote: I don't think we're yet in the super data rich regime. So, I think in our case these hybrid models might be still the thing to go for

insights.claim: Theis predicts that in the long run the most-used biology models will be flexible, data-driven ones with interpretation added a posteriori, citing AlphaFold, where later versions learned rotation symmetry from data rather than having it built in.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Data scale ultimately beats hand-engineered biology priors, favoring whoever owns the biggest datasets.
insights.quote: at some point data beats human-made additional concepts in these models.

insights.claim: Early single-cell foundation model papers failed to demonstrate scaling laws, producing an overhyped phase followed by a sobering-up; reviewers now demand proper scaling-law evidence before buying in.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Scrutinize bio foundation-model claims for demonstrated scaling behavior.
insights.quote: people haven't really shown that you need this complexity to actually sort of really scale up.

insights.claim: Theis lab's contrastive model scConcept (SE concept) shows strong scaling: the paper compared against Geneformer at ~30 million cells, and a Hugging Face release uses 350 million cells across 16 species with up to ~100 million parameters, with nice scaling behavior starting to emerge.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Single-cell models are beginning to show scaling behavior at hundreds of millions of cells, approaching a data-driven regime.
insights.quote: on on Hugging Face now, we have a 350 million cell model with I think going up to maybe 100 million parameters

insights.claim: Self-supervised learning for single-cell data is still unsettled: approaches copy NLP masked autoencoders, tabular foundation models, JEPA-style and contrastive methods, with losses and representations still debated.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: No dominant architecture yet, so technical moats in model design are fragile.

themes.theme: Virtual cells as world models and baselines

insights.claim: Theis frames a perturbation-prediction virtual cell as a world model f(x, a) that predicts next state x' from state x and action a; representation learning learns the state space, but a separate generative model (e.g. flow matching) is needed to push forward along the action.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Pure foundation-model embeddings are not enough for perturbation prediction; generative dynamics layers are required.
insights.quote: it's not just a model that is sort of f of x, but f of x {comma} a, right?

insights.claim: Theis lab's CellFlow paper (accepted at Nature Methods) shows flow-matching approaches are much better at generating perturbation effects, but depend heavily on a good latent space.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Flow matching on strong latent spaces is emerging as the leading perturbation-prediction recipe.

insights.claim: For cell type prediction within an organ, near state-of-the-art models are still logistic regression (Theis's paper was titled 'Deep learning is not needed for cell type prediction'), whereas cross-organ prediction benefits from nonlinear models like scTab.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Many bio-AI tasks do not need deep learning; value depends on task difficulty.
insights.quote: it turns out that even nowadays, I think some close to state-of-the-art models are really just logistic regression

insights.claim: In the Arc Institute's Virtual Cell Challenge, some metrics were exploitable, and once exploitation was removed the real winning model was flow-matching based, showing nonlinearities are needed for complex perturbation tasks.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Benchmarks in virtual-cell AI can be gamed; headline leaderboard wins need scrutiny.
insights.quote: Dark one is also fixed a bunch of metrics that weren't even so so single cell specific and they could be just just exploited.

insights.claim: For simple cell-line gene knockouts with subtle effects, complex models often overfit noisy data, so linear baselines or even predicting the mean remain hard to beat.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Claims of AI superiority in perturbation prediction should be checked against mean and linear baselines.
insights.quote: better than the mean is sometimes not as hard if there are so much noise in the data and this stuff is super noisy.

insights.claim: Predicting neighboring cells' gene expression from a single cell's state (a task introduced in the Nicheformer spatial foundation model paper) is harder and requires stronger nonlinear models and subtler data.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Harder spatial tasks are where large models can justify themselves over baselines.

insights.claim: Theis expects agents/AutoML to eventually try out all algorithmic combinations, so the highest-value human contribution becomes formulating the right metric; co-host noted a Bo Wang Nature paper showing metric choice explained some linear-baseline wins.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: As model search is automated, problem/metric definition becomes the scarce skill.
insights.quote: what maybe our biggest ideas go into is actually this metric formulation

themes.theme: Business models: platform vs drugs vs data moats

insights.claim: Theis has repeatedly seen 'foundation model of biology' platform companies, attractive to investors, pivot to developing drugs because platform monetization is unclear, especially in the more conservative European VC ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Pure AI-bio platform plays face a monetization gap that typically forces a drug-asset pivot.
insights.quote: I saw so many of these platform companies pivoting at some point to we make a drug.

insights.claim: There is fear that frontier AI labs (an 'Astra 2.0'-type model) might commoditize parts of the virtual cell business anyway.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Model-only bio startups carry platform-commoditization risk from big AI labs.

insights.claim: Host RJ Honicky notes that this year the pattern has reversed in structural biology, with model/tools companies (e.g. Boltz) and RL-environment plays staying platform-focused, and he wants similar activity in virtual cells like Noetik.
insights.speaker: RJ Honicky (host)
insights.so_what: Investor appetite for pure AI-bio tools companies may be returning, starting in structural biology.

insights.claim: Theis argues the sweet spot where pharma actually buys in is coupling models with unique data generation; his group set up a Cancer Organoid Perturbation Atlas consortium with pharma partners who pay for early access to perturbation datasets.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Proprietary data generation, not the model alone, is the defensible moat in virtual-cell companies.
insights.quote: if you couple it with data generation not just with the modeling part, I think this is where sweet spot hits where then also actually farmer gets buying.

insights.claim: Nvidia hired two of Theis's people within one month a few months ago as it builds up a computation-plus-biology effort, with other big tech companies doing similar.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Big tech is actively building bio-AI teams and competing for cross-domain talent.
insights.quote: I think Nvidia just a few months ago were hired in 1 month two of my people

insights.claim: Theis lab is releasing Lab Compass on bioRxiv, an inverse generative model that, given a forward world model, tells experimenters what to do to reach a target cell state; it was validated with three to four lab-in-the-loop cycles with a University of Cambridge hematopoiesis collaborator.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: The field is moving from mapping and prediction to actively steering experiments.
insights.quote: lab compass, which is an inverse generative model that actually allows you once you have a forward world model or whatever to tell you what you need to do in order to reach a certain state.

insights.claim: Despite big pharma promoting lab-in-the-loop as a theme, few real examples run multiple iterative loops, because choosing the optimal next experiment is non-trivial and experimentalists resist investing long experiments in strange model-suggested conditions.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Organizational culture, not just modeling, is the bottleneck to closed-loop AI discovery.
insights.quote: there's not many examples that where really people do multiple [clears throat] loops of this integration

insights.claim: Theis thinks robotics for cell-level lab automation is a tad too early because assay cycle times are still long; current practice is closer to active learning, with RL on the full loop the ultimate vision.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Lab-robotics bets for cell biology may be early; assay speed is the gating factor.
insights.quote: A lot of people then start throwing around robotics and so on as well but I I think this is a tad too early because the the cycle times in terms of our essays are still a bit on the long side

insights.claim: Theis sees computational startups that use perturbation world models to drive experiments and data generation (lab in the loop) as the next generation of startups.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Closed-loop experiment-steering companies are an emerging startup category.

insights.claim: Helmholtz, possibly Europe's largest research organization by funding, hosts the Computational Health Center at Helmholtz Munich with roughly 45 group leaders and 500-600 people, which Theis calls Europe's largest academic health-AI research site, aiming at a 'virtual human'.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Munich is a concentrated talent pool for health-AI spinouts.
insights.quote: maybe 45 group leaders and professors and maybe 500 to 600 people now

insights.claim: Theis says the EU creates about as many startups as the US and Munich leads Germany, but Europe drops off at scaling because large risk-taking VCs for Series A/B rounds are scarce, pushing founders to the US.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: European deep-tech offers early-stage deal flow but a growth-capital gap that US investors can fill.
insights.quote: The thing is where Europe and particular also Germany drops off is at the scaling part.

insights.claim: Theis describes Munich as perhaps continental Europe's prime place for VC and deep tech, with bio and defense especially exploding.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Munich bio and defense tech is a European hotspot worth tracking.

insights.claim: Theis told every PI and group leader in his department he expects at least one spin-off within the next three years.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: A near-term pipeline of Munich computational-bio spinouts is likely.
insights.quote: every every PI every group leader, I would expect you to at least to have one one one spin-off in in in the next 3 years.

insights.claim: EU regulation such as the AI Act complicates health data access across hospitals, but Finland (FinnGen) and Denmark have strong linked population records, and the European Health Data Space should require cross-border health record linkage within roughly two years.
insights.speaker: Fabian Theis
insights.so_what: Cross-border EU health data access may open up, but slower than visions suggest.
